subtitle.en: A careful look at what ancient writers, excavations, and genetic studies can be asked, and at the limits those records do not cross.

shortDescription.en: The book examines the people Greek and Latin writers called Dacians and Getae through written sources, archaeological remains, and genetic studies. Its scope runs from classical names and scattered language evidence, through Carpathian and lower Danube centuries before a named kingdom, to fortress building, the wars, and the later Roman province. A central question is how far ancient authors, excavated places, and sampled genomes can carry an account of named communities, a kingdom confronted by Rome, settlement, ancestry, and arguments about continuity. Thematic tensions arise around whether a shared classical name, frontier religious stories, mountain sanctuaries, Roman war narratives, provincial inscriptions, and genetic samples from different centuries and landscapes belong in one account. Those records leave open what written testimony, excavation, and genetic comparison can and cannot answer about cult, language, political power, population movement, and any present-day link with the ancient communities.

en: A careful look at what ancient writers, excavations, and genetic studies can be asked, and at the limits those records do not cross.
Greek and Latin writers left a name for communities and a kingdom Rome later conquered. The request behind this book was narrow enough that a continuous national biography would change the task.

Two emperors fought the wars treated here as the best dated events, yet they remain Roman events. A bridge or an imperial column still invites a match that may not hold. Ancient DNA, the newest record, is the easiest to overread.

What can the names, the language, and the early written descriptions actually carry, and can an ancient geographer's sentence serve as a map? Can earlier histories of settlement and fortified hills be compressed into a single people waiting to be named? Was the kingdom ethnically uniform, or only named that way by a foreign state?
Was the Roman capital north of the Danube the same place as the old royal center? What can a genome not show about a language or a modern nation? Did the name move when administration ended?
The account separates a confirmed finding from a plausible reading and from a story the evidence does not yet support. Ancient authors, excavation, and genome-wide ancient DNA are set side by side.
Excavation reports and a LiDAR study are asked whether they close the larger arguments, while ancient accounts, archaeology, and genetics stay in separate groups so their weight remains visible.

It is for general readers, students, teachers, and researchers who want genetic claims and continuity debates held to the same standard as texts and excavations, and who want ancient history argued from its own evidence. That standard is the invitation, and also the limit of the promise.

Ancient DNA is the newest of the three records and the easiest to overread, and later centuries have been asked to do modern work in arguments about continuity. Was the Roman capital the old royal center, and did the name move when administration ended?

What can a genome not show about a language or a modern nation, and did the name move when administration ended? The newest record is the easiest to overread, and later centuries are still being asked to do modern work in arguments about continuity.
